idiom_name: records for values, sealed interface + exhaustive switch for decisions
implementation_notes: Java 17 supplies the two primitives the split needs: `record` for immutable inputs and results (value equality, no setters, `List.copyOf` in a compact constructor) and a `sealed interface` with an exhaustive `switch` expression for the decision space, so 'what should happen' is a value the shell matches on. The classic layered service with injected repositories is replaced by a static pure method that takes the loaded records plus the facts the shell learned (`boolean member`, an injected `Clock`) and returns a `PriceResult`; expected failures are values (`Optional`, or a sealed outcome), not exceptions. Keep the service shape only where the logic really is a conversation with the world.
pitfalls: Records are shallowly immutable: a `List<PriceItem>` component is still a mutable list the caller can change (and `List.of` does not copy), so copy on the way in and expose `List.copyOf` on the way out.

An exhaustive `switch` over a sealed interface must not carry a `default` branch - adding it hides the compile error that tells every interpreter a new permitted variant arrived (which is the mechanism's value).
`Instant.now()`, `UUID.randomUUID()` and `System.getenv()` compile anywhere; pass a `Clock`/values in, and remember that the shell's `Clock.systemUTC()` is the only place time is allowed to enter.

variants.name: Hand-written immutable value classes (Java 8)
variants.idiom_name: final classes with final fields, defensive copies, static pure methods
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 8/11 the same split is written by hand: final classes with final fields, a constructor that validates and defensively copies collections (`Collections.unmodifiableList`), no setters, and static methods that return new instances; the decision space becomes an enum or a small class hierarchy with `instanceof`/visitor-style checks instead of a sealed interface with pattern matching. The shell is unchanged: a servlet or controller loads, calls the static method and applies the result. Choose this only when the runtime really is pre-17 - on 17+ records and sealed types express the same design with less code and compiler-checked exhaustiveness.
pitfalls: `final` protects the reference, not the object: a `final List` field is still mutable unless wrapped with `Collections.unmodifiableList`, and `unmodifiable*` is a view of the original, not a copy.

Without records there is no `equals`/`hashCode`/`toString` unless you write them, so value semantics leak into every comparison and test assertion; generate them (IDE/Lombok) or use the enum/`Optional` shapes where equality matters.

`java.util.Optional` is designed for return values, not as a general monad: using it for control flow in the core produces nested `Optional`s and `get()` calls in the shell - return an explicit outcome class instead.
